newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels set deadline in tense Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rebels set deadline in tense Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Peruvian guerrillas holding about 200 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence gave the government one hour on Wednesday to bow to their demands after an explosion and gunfire rocked the building.

The Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, who stormed the residence on Tuesday night, threatened to kill all their hostages -- including top diplomats -- unless the government freed jailed comrades.

"Up to now there is no harm but within an hour they (the hostages) could suffer harm. We only give him (Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori) one hour more," a guerrrilla spokesman told a local television station.
"If within an hour the president does not communicate with us he will see the results," he said. The ultimatum was issued at 11:15 a.m. (1615 GMT).

A rebel spokesman told a local television station 20 minutes later: "We want to speak with him (Fujimori) within half an hour." Asked what the rebels intended to do if the deadline was not met, he said: "We will start to take lives."

Shortly before the ultimatum, an explosion was heard in the residence, immediately followed by shots. It was not clear if the shots came from the MRTA guerrillas within the embassy or from policemen outside, but a police officer told Reuters the explosion was probably a publicity stunt by the MRTA.

The rebels stormed the building on Tuesday at around 8 p.m local time (0100 GMT), firing a rocket from outside. About 20 rebels swarmed into the residence through a hole blasted in an outside wall, witnesses and officials said. Some unconfirmed reports said guerrillas disguised as waiters joined them from the inside.

At least one MRTA member suffered a gunshot wound in the leg during a chaotic shootout with police and security guards, who fired into the residence from nearby buildings following the initial assault. No injuries to hostages were reported.
Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed the rebels smuggled ammunition into the residence among flowers and Christmas cake.
Speaking to local media from the building, rebels accused the Peruvian government of "intransigence" and said they had laid explosive booby-traps at entrances to the building.

"Up to now, there is an intransigent position (from the authorities). The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza said, adding that the rebels wanted transportation for them and the freed prisoners to a guerrilla-controlled area in the country's jungle.

At around 10:20 a.m. local time (1520 GMT), the rebels demanded that Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, personally join in negotiations. The president so far had not commented publicly on the attack but in a conversation with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto he said Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila was handling negotiations.

Foreign nations with ambassadors inside the building have urged Fujimori to do everything in his power to protect the hostages and not use force to flush out the rebels. Japan, Germany and Austria, Panama, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil and Cuba confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages and various reports also said Spain, South Korea and the European Community had ambassadors inside.
Among Peruvian hostages were Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja and at least three local legislators.

The MRTA guerrillas, who called the operation "Breaking The Silence," claimed they still held 250 hostages after the release of about 80 women and old people. One of those released, Sally Bowen, the president of Peru's foreign correspondents' association, said "between 250 and 300" men were still being held inside shortly after midnight local time (0500 GMT).

The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and their highest priority was the release of Victor Polay, their leader who was imprisoned in 1992. They also called for a review of Peru's judicial system and direct negotiations with the government beginning at dawn on Wednesday.

The released hostages, who included Fujimori's mother apparently freed by mistake, rushed out of the residence dazed and crying. "They are freeing us to show that they are not doing us any harm," one woman said.
Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki offered to remain as the only hostage but that was refused by the rebels, Bowen said.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war on communist rebels belonging to the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.
